draft.title: Competition policy
card: Competition policy is a set of laws that keep markets competitive. Competition pushes firms to keep prices low and to improve quality, which benefits consumers.
In Australia the main law is the Competition and Consumer Act 2010. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) enforces it.
The law bans anti-competitive conduct, such as competing firms agreeing to fix prices. It also bans a firm with a lot of market power from using that power to shut out rivals.

The ACCC can take firms to court, and the court can order penalties. The ACCC also reviews proposed mergers, which are deals where firms join, and can oppose those that would greatly reduce competition.
draft.remember: Competition policy uses law to stop firms from cutting out competition.

a.q: Three petrol stations in a country town secretly agree to charge the same high price. Which part of competition policy does this breach?
opts: The ban on price fixing between competing firms
The ban on firms advertising their prices
The rule that firms must charge the lowest price
The ban on firms operating in small towns
a.why: Competing firms agreeing on prices is price fixing, which the law bans because it removes competition. Firms are not required to charge the lowest price, and advertising prices is not the issue.
a.clue: Think about what the three firms agreed to do together.

b.q: Two large Australian supermarket chains plan to merge. The ACCC finds it would leave shoppers with almost no choice in many suburbs. What can the ACCC do?
opts: Oppose the merger because it would reduce competition
Approve it because larger firms always cut prices
Set the prices the merged firm must charge
Ignore it because mergers are not covered by the law
b.why: The ACCC reviews mergers and can oppose those that would greatly reduce competition. It does not set prices for the firm, and larger firms do not always cut prices. Mergers are covered by the law.
b.clue: The ACCC looks at what a merger does to competition.

a.best: The ban on price fixing between competing firms

b.best: Oppose the merger because it would reduce competition

proposal.title: Competition policy
card: Competition policy is a set of laws that keep markets competitive, which pushes firms to keep prices low and quality high. In Australia the main law is the Competition and Consumer Act 2010, enforced by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC).
Price fixing is banned: competing firms cannot agree on the prices they charge. A single firm setting a high price on its own is not price fixing.
A firm with a lot of market power also cannot misuse it in ways that greatly reduce competition, such as squeezing smaller rivals out of the market.

The ACCC can take firms to court, and the court can order penalties. The ACCC also reviews proposed mergers, which are deals where firms join, and can oppose those that would greatly reduce competition.
proposal.remember: Competition policy uses law to stop firms from cutting out competition.

a.q: Three petrol stations in a country town secretly agree to charge the same high price. Why does this breach competition law?
opts: Competing firms agreed on a price instead of competing
One firm misused its market power to shut out rivals
The firms merged in a way that reduced competition
The firms charged a price well above their costs
a.why: The breach is the agreement: rival firms set their price together rather than competing, which is price fixing. A high price alone is not illegal, and no single firm misused its power or merged with another.
a.clue: Focus on what the three firms did together.

b.q: Two large Australian supermarket chains plan to merge. The ACCC finds it would leave shoppers with almost no choice in many suburbs. What can the ACCC do?
opts: Oppose the merger because it would reduce competition
Approve it because larger firms always cut prices
Set the prices the merged firm must charge
Ignore it because mergers are not covered by the law
b.why: The ACCC reviews mergers and can oppose those that would greatly reduce competition. It does not set prices for the firm, and larger firms do not always cut prices. Mergers are covered by the law.
b.clue: The ACCC looks at what a merger does to competition.
